title: Managed Kubernetes (EKS / GKE / AKS)
summary: Build it yourself or hand it off: what managed offerings take over, and what stays yours.

sections.heading: What production asks of a cluster

blocks.text: A one-ship training harbor is charming until its only office floods: then everything stops. A real port plans ahead. It keeps the harbor office (control plane) apart from the fleet, runs copies of each office desk with callers spread across the front desks, and keeps enough ships ready. It plans for busy and quiet seasons, and in a shared port it issues badges (RBAC) and cargo limits so no tenant hogs the docks.
A single-machine learning cluster has a single point of failure. A production cluster has to plan for:

items: **Availability**: separate the control plane from worker nodes, replicate control plane components, load-balance traffic to the API server, and keep enough worker nodes available.
**Scale**: plan for growing or seasonal demand on both the control plane and the workers, and for scaling down unused capacity.
**Security and access**: shared clusters need RBAC and other mechanisms, plus limits on what users and workloads can consume.

blocks.text: Before building an office yourself, consider letting the city (a cloud provider) run parts of the port. It can carry cargo with no port for you to manage, billing by the cargo you declare (serverless). It can staff and patch the harbor office (managed control plane), keep your chosen fleets seaworthy (managed worker nodes), or connect the port to warehouses, depots and ID offices. Even if the city runs the office, you still decide how your ships are managed.
Before building production yourself, the docs suggest considering **Turnkey Cloud Solutions** providers or other Kubernetes partners. The options are:

rows: Running workloads without you managing a cluster at all; billed for CPU, memory and disk requests
Scale and availability of the control plane, plus patches and upgrades
Keeping your configured node pools available and ready for upgrades
Connecting Kubernetes to storage, registries, auth and dev tools

blocks.text: Even with a managed control plane, you still have to decide how to manage your worker nodes.

Building the port yourself means a long checklist. Hire a construction crew such as `kubeadm`, kops or kubespray. Manage the seals (certificates) on office mail. Put a traffic marshal (load balancer) in front of the front desks. Keep the master ledger (`etcd`) separate if needed and photocopy it into the safe regularly. Run several office systems, each service on at least three machines if systemd runs it, and consider spreading across districts (zones).

items: Choose deployment tools, such as **kubeadm**, kops or kubespray.
Manage the certificates that secure control plane communication.
Put a load balancer in front of the API server instances.
Separate etcd if needed, and **back it up regularly**.
Run multiple control plane systems. If they run under an init service such as systemd, run each service on at least three machines.
Consider spreading the cluster across multiple zones.

blocks.text: Managed offerings give real-world context. For hands-on cluster setup practice, study the kubeadm topic.

In the Amazon district, the city's port service is EKS. On the standard plan, AWS staffs the harbor office (control plane) while you crew your own ships. On Auto Mode, the city runs the ships too (the data plane). Badges there work two ways at once: Kubernetes' own badge system combined with the city's ID office, AWS IAM. It is a handy example of the city running the office for you.

items: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) is AWS's managed Kubernetes service.
**EKS standard**: AWS manages the Kubernetes control plane.
**EKS Auto Mode**: EKS also manages the nodes (the data plane).
Access control combines Kubernetes features with AWS IAM.

blocks.text: In the Google district the service is GKE, and every ship is a Compute Engine VM. In **Autopilot** mode the city runs both the harbor office and the ships, and you pay only for the cargo weight your running bays declare (Pod requests). In **Standard** mode you pay for whole ships, full or half empty, regardless of what your bays declare.

items: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) is Google Cloud's managed implementation of Kubernetes. Nodes are Compute Engine VMs.
**Autopilot mode**: Google Cloud manages both the nodes and the control plane, and you pay for the compute resources your running Pods request.
**Standard mode**: you pay for all resources on your nodes, regardless of Pod requests.

sections.heading: Example: Azure AKS
sections.sourceTitle: What is Azure Kubernetes Service? (Microsoft docs)

blocks.text: In the Azure district the service is AKS. Azure builds and configures your harbor office (control plane) at no cost; you pay for the ships carrying your cargo. With **AKS Automatic**, Azure also looks after the ships, scaling, security, monitoring and upgrades. With **AKS Standard**, you configure the port and manage your fleets (node pools) yourself. City prices and perks change often, so check the vendor page before relying on any detail.

items: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is Azure's managed Kubernetes service.
When you create a cluster, Azure creates and configures the control plane at no cost. You pay for the nodes that run your applications.
**AKS Automatic**: Azure handles node management, scaling, security, monitoring and upgrades.
**AKS Standard**: you control cluster configuration and manage node pools yourself.
